G0871.detail: 1. The verb literally means "to make similar" or "to render similar." In its only biblical usage, it applies to Melchizedek: he is described as "made similar to the Son of God" (Hebrews 7:3). The apostle Paul uses this word to say that Melchizedek, in his biblical presentation, resembles the Son in certain traits — he has no father, mother, or genealogy mentioned, as if his existence were forever comparable to that of the eternal Son.
G0871.origine: The word is formed from the prefix ἀφό (apo, "from") and the verb ὁμοιόω (homoioō, "to make similar"), itself derived from the adjective ὅμοιος (homoios, "similar"). This root refers to the fundamental idea of resemblance or similarity. The Greek word ὁμοία also appears in several passages of the New Testament to mean "like" or "of the same nature."
G0871.emploi: The verb ἀφομοιόω appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 7:3. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews uses it to shed light on the mystery of Melchizedek, this character from Genesis and Psalm 110 of whom the Bible gives no genealogy, birth date, or death date. By saying that Melchizedek is "made similar" to the Son of God, Paul suggests that this absence of genealogical details makes Melchizedek a figure resembling the Son — a resemblance that illuminates the eternal and unending nature of his priesthood.
G0871.portee: This word invites the reader to see how the Bible itself, through what it says and what it leaves unsaid, prepares the way for understanding Jesus Christ. The resemblance between Melchizedek and the Son emphasizes that Christ's priesthood transcends any human genealogical succession: it is eternal and of a completely different order. It is a beautiful invitation to recognize how the Old Testament speaks of Christ, not through literal predictions, but through mysterious correspondences.

sens: Fix one's attention on something
Direct one's gaze or thoughts toward a specific point
Perceive or ascertain something by seeing
G0872.detail:
1. The verb ἀφοράω expresses the action of completely focusing one's attention on something, turning the gaze away from everything else. In Hebrews 12:2, believers are urged to "look to Jesus" — not just a glance, but a fixation of the gaze and soul on Him as the source and perfecter of faith.

2. More broadly, the word means to voluntarily direct one's attention toward an object or direction. In Philippians 2:23, Paul says he will "see the outcome" of his situation: it involves clearly perceiving how the situation will unfold by paying attention to what is developing.

3. Finally, in a simpler sense, it simply means "to see" or "to ascertain" — not a passive vision, but an active, intentional perception.
G0872.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἀπό ("away from, from") and οράω ("to see"). The basic image is that of turning or distancing the gaze from everything else to focus on a single target. It is a verb of vision that emphasizes the direction and concentration of the gaze, rather than the simple act of seeing.
G0872.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Hebrews 12:2, it denotes the action of fixing the gaze and soul on Jesus as a model of faith — a total spiritual concentration. In Philippians 2:23, Paul uses it in the simpler sense of "to perceive" or "to ascertain" the outcome of his captivity, meaning to see how it will resolve. Both uses retain the idea of directed, intentional vision.
G0872.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that "looking" in biblical faith is not a distracted attention, but a fixation of heart and mind. In Hebrews 12:2, it calls to turn one's gaze away from every obstacle to focus solely on Jesus — a lesson in perseverance in faith amid trials. It is a call to spiritual vigilance and the absolute priority given to Christ.

sens: Mark a boundary, divide a space or group into two distinct parts
Remove someone from a group, cast them out or exclude them
Set apart for a function, service, or special consecration
G0873.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to draw a boundary that divides. Jesus describes the final judgment where the angels will "separate" the wicked from the righteous (Matthew 13:49), and the shepherd "separates" the sheep from the goats by placing them on his right or left (Matthew 25:32). It is an action of clear and definitive division.

2. The word also denotes the exclusion or rejection of a person from a community. Luke 6:22 speaks of those who will be "cast out" — literally separated from the synagogue — because of Christ. Paul "separated" the disciples from the synagogue of Damascus to teach them apart (Acts 19:9), thus creating a distinct group. It is a social rupture.

3. Finally, "to separate" can mean to set someone aside for a special service: Paul was "set apart" (literally "separated") to proclaim the Gospel (Romans 1:1). In Galatians 1:15, it conveys the same idea: God "separated" him from his mother's womb, consecrating him for a mission. Here, separation is an honor, a divine calling.
G0873.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "apo-" (away from, out of) and "horizô" (to draw a boundary, to set a limit). This is why it fundamentally means to draw a boundary or separation. In Greek, the root "horizô" is found in "horizon," which marks the limit between heaven and earth. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates several Hebrew verbs meaning to separate, to remove, or to set apart.
G0873.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and the Gospels. Matthew uses it twice to describe definitive separations at judgment (13:49; 25:32). Luke uses it for exclusion from the synagogue (6:22). Paul employs it to describe either a practical exclusion (Acts 19:9) or his own consecration to God's service (Romans 1:1; Galatians 1:15). In 2 Corinthians 6:17, Paul urges believers to "separate" themselves from unbelievers — a moral separation. In Galatians 2:12, he reports that Peter "drew back" from the Gentiles, separating himself from them out of fear. Everywhere, the word expresses a cut, either in the sense of judgment, exclusion, or consecration.
G0873.portee: This word teaches that God establishes separations: between good and evil on the day of judgment, between the people of God and moral impurity, and between those He calls for a holy mission. For the believer, it challenges: are we ready to be "separated" from what distracts us from God? It also reminds that consecration to God involves a separation — not out of pride or disdain, but out of faithfulness to the calling received.

sens: Starting point, basis for action
Circumstance that arises, opportunity
Motive or reason that one seizes to act
Pretext or excuse used
G0874.detail:
1. Originally, the word denotes a starting point or a base — like a military base from which an expedition departs. This is the most concrete sense of the term.

2. By extension, it denotes a favorable circumstance that arises and can be seized to act: an opportunity. This is the sense Paul uses when speaking of giving "occasion" to boast (2 Corinthians 5:12).

3. The word also takes on the meaning of motive or incitement — something that drives one to do something. Thus, sin "seizes the occasion" of the commandment to produce covetousness (Romans 7:8): the commandment becomes the motive or pretext for sin.

4. Sometimes the word denotes a pretext or excuse — a reason invoked to justify one's action, often dishonestly. Paul refuses to give an "occasion" to those who seek to boast (2 Corinthians 11:12), and young women should not give the adversary an "occasion" to slander (1 Timothy 5:14).
G0874.origine: The word is composed of "apo" (away, out) and "hormê" (impulse, impetus). It properly describes what gives the signal to depart, what sets in motion. In Greek military vocabulary, it designated the base from which the army launches an attack. The family of the word includes "hormê" (impulse, movement) and "hormaô" (to rush, to spring forth). The Hebrew word "hamon" (noise, tumult, agitated crowd) that the Greek "aphormê" translates in Ezekiel 5:7 shows how a circumstance can be a catalyst, a trigger.
G0874.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. In the letters to the Romans and Corinthians, Paul uses it to describe how a circumstance can become an incitement to evil or an excuse for an action: sin seizes the occasion of the commandment (Romans 7:8, 11), Christian freedom should not be a pretext for the flesh (Galatians 5:13), young women should not give occasion to the slanderer (1 Timothy 5:14). The word can also denote a neutral or positive opportunity — that of recommending or glorifying someone (2 Corinthians 5:12). The dominant nuance is that of pretext or reason that one seizes, often to the detriment of another.
G0874.portee: This word sheds light on an important spiritual truth: our circumstances and freedoms can become traps if we divert them from their purpose. The frequency with which Paul speaks of "giving occasion" to sin or to the adversary reminds the Christian that their responsibility extends beyond their intentions to what they offer as pretext or reason for wrongdoing. It is an invitation to vigilance in the use of Christian freedom and to be mindful not to cause others to stumble.

sens: To let foam flow from the mouth
To manifest extreme agitation or violence
G0875.detail:
1. To foam means to produce whitish froth at the mouth — a sign of violent convulsion or serious illness. In Mark 9:18, the possessed child "foams": his body undergoes contractions that cause this foam to come from his mouth, while he grinds his teeth and becomes stiff. It is a terrifying symptom, showing the demon's grip on his body.
2. Figuratively, to foam expresses uncontrolled agitation or violence. In Mark 9:20, when the demon sees Jesus, the spirit "violently threw him into convulsions" and the child "was rolling around foaming": the verb describes not only the physical symptom but also the rage and fury of the demon in the face of the One who will cast it out.
G0875.origine: The word comes from the Greek aphros, "foam" or "froth." This foam is visible on the troubled sea, but also — as the biblical text shows — on the mouth of one who is undergoing a violent convulsion. It is a concrete verb, directly derived from the observation of the physical world.
G0875.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Mark 9, during the account of the young boy possessed by a mute spirit. In verses 18 and 20, it describes the same phenomenon: the convulsions that seize the child when the demon torments him. Mark chooses this raw and vivid verb to show the violence of the illness and the power of the demon controlling this body. It is a medical and dramatic detail that only Mark reports.
G0875.portee: This word reminds us that the work of demons in the real world manifests through the destruction of body and spirit. Jesus does not cast out abstractions, but He frees a tortured child. The detail of the foam makes the miracle tangible and shows Jesus' compassion in the face of concrete physical suffering.

sens: White bubbles or froth that form on the surface of disturbed water
Foamy saliva that bursts from the mouth during convulsions or rage
G0876.detail: 1. Foam is that light white froth that covers the water of the sea or a turbulent stream: it forms when the water is violently disturbed. 2. In a man or animal in the grip of a violent fit (convulsion, rage), the saliva becomes foamy and bursts from the mouth. In Luke 9:39, the demon possessing the child makes him foam: this terrifying symptom shows the violence of the evil that shakes and tears him apart.
G0876.origine: The Greek word aphros literally refers to the foam of the sea or rivers (it appears in ancient Greek texts like the Iliad). It evokes the image of extreme agitation and loss of control: when something foams, it is because a brute force is raging within it. The Greeks also used it to describe the saliva of a furious beast or a man in crisis.
G0876.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 9:39, to describe a symptom of demonic possession. The possessed child "foams," which means that his mouth expels foamy saliva during his convulsions. This brutal detail shows how the Gospel reports without hesitation the visible symptoms of the demon's power over a person. The foam is not just a noise or a cry: it is a physical phenomenon that reveals the extreme violence of the crisis.
G0876.portee: By describing the child who foams, Luke shows us the raw reality of demonic possession: it is not a metaphor, but a physical affliction that dehumanizes the victim and demonstrates the destructive nature of evil. This detail helps us understand the urgency and gravity of Jesus' request and the importance of His victory over the demon.

sens: Lack of common sense, judgment, wisdom
Irresponsible or unreasonable behavior
Behavior that provokes shame or ridicule
In a spiritual sense: moral deviation or rejection of divine truth
G0877.detail:
1. Foolishness is the absence of wisdom and discernment — the opposite of common sense. In Mark 7:22, it appears in a list of sins that defile a person, alongside theft and slander: it denotes this lack of judgment that leads one to act against their own conscience.
2. It also describes reckless or senseless behavior, as when the apostle Paul says he speaks in "foolishness" to justify himself (2 Corinthians 11:1, 11:17): he acknowledges that boasting, even for a just cause, borders on ridicule in the eyes of the world.
3. It can evoke the shame and dishonor attached to impudence or misplaced boldness: in 2 Corinthians 11:21, Paul speaks "as a fool" to dare to match his opponents in boldness, a statement he himself finds unreasonable.
4. In its spiritual depth, foolishness opposes the wisdom of God: it is the moral deviation of a person who turns away from the truth and acts against their own conscience or against God's order.
G0877.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἄφρων ("without wisdom"), composed of the privative prefix ἀ- ("without") and a root related to wisdom. In ancient Greek, it often translates the Hebrew אִוֶּלֶת (foolishness) and נְבָלָה (foolishness, wickedness), words that in the Old Testament denote moral stupidity — the state of one who refuses to listen to divine wisdom. Biblical foolishness is never merely a lack of intelligence, but always a sin: the refusal to submit to God and His law.
G0877.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, only in Paul. In Mark 7:22, it comes from the heart of man and renders him impure, alongside covetousness or deceit. In 2 Corinthians 11, Paul uses it three times: he speaks of "foolishness" to denote the attitude of one who boasts or compares themselves to others, which contradicts Christian humility. However, to refute the false apostles, Paul accepts to "speak as a fool," that is, to resort to the same boasting as his opponents — a paradox he himself highlights. Thus, foolishness, for Paul, is what comes from the mouth of the wicked heart, or what one adopts against their nature to combat the pride of others.
G0877.portee: This word invites the reader to examine their own heart and thoughts: moral foolishness arises from within, from the refusal to follow God's wisdom. It warns us that boasting or seeking human approval is foolish from a spiritual perspective. At the same time, Paul's sincerity when he "speaks in foolishness" for his defense shows that sometimes, one must adopt the methods of the world to reveal their absurdity — but always remaining clear-headed and recognizing that it is unreasonable.

sens: lacking reason and judgment
acting without considering the consequences
ignoring or despising divine wisdom
spiritually blind or closed to the truth
G0878.detail:
1. The fool is one who does not use reason, who acts without thinking. When Jesus calls the rich man who accumulates treasures without thinking of death a "fool" (Luke 12:20), he refers to someone who acts without discernment, forgetting what is essential.
2. It is also one who commits unreasonable and thoughtless acts. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:36 refers to a fool as someone who would claim that seeds never die: he rebukes a foolish statement that contradicts the obvious.
3. It is one who deliberately rejects or ignores wisdom and teaching. In Romans 2:20, Paul speaks of the teacher of fools, meaning one who must instruct people lacking good sense.
4. Often in the New Testament, the fool is one who refuses to acknowledge God or His will. In Ephesians 5:17, not understanding what the Lord's will is is to behave like a fool.
G0878.origine: The Greek word ἄφρων comes from the negation (the prefix ἀ-, "without") and φρήν (phrên), which refers to the mind, the seat of reflection and good sense. A fool is literally someone without critical thinking, without discernment. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament translates terms like כְּסִיל (kesil, the fool) and נָבָל (naval, the senseless), which all describe one who lacks wisdom before God.
G0878.emploi: This word appears ten times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and the Gospels. Jesus uses it to denounce the rich fool who forgets that he will die (Luke 12:20) and the pride of the Pharisees who do not understand God's intention (Luke 11:40). Paul uses it to criticize those who reject the Resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:36) or who judge him a fool for boasting about his visions (2 Corinthians 11-12). Each time, the word denotes not mere intellectual foolishness, but spiritual blindness: one who refuses to see God or His truth. In 2 Corinthians 11:19, Paul notes that the Corinthians tolerate fools while they themselves think they are wise — which reveals their own folly.
G0878.portee: This word reminds us that true wisdom is not a matter of raw intelligence, but of communion with God. The fool is not one who ignores mathematics, but one who lives as if God does not exist or as if His words have no weight. For the Christian, the text invites us to continually seek divine wisdom (Ephesians 5:17) and to recognize how foolish we can be without the fear of the Lord and listening to His Word.

sens: To fall into sleep
To succumb to sleep despite the circumstances
G0879.detail:
1. To fall asleep simply means to transition from wakefulness to sleep. It is the natural action of dozing off when the body and mind rest.

2. In the Gospel, the word describes Jesus falling asleep in the boat in the middle of the lake while the disciples are sailing (Luke 8:23). The sleep occurs despite the jolts of navigation and the task at hand: it is a deep immersion in rest, indifferent to the context. The word emphasizes not only the act of falling asleep but the state of sleep attained despite everything.
G0879.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ὑπνόω, which means "to make sleep" or "to put to sleep." The prefix ἀφ- (apo-, "away from") changes the meaning: the verb shifts from the active sense "to make sleep" to the middle or passive sense "to fall asleep." The initial image is that of sleep overtaking the body, like a force that invades it.
G0879.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 8:23. Jesus falls asleep in the boat while the disciples sail. This unique occurrence reveals a moment of humanity: Jesus, exhausted from His ministry, falls deeply asleep. The context—a storm arising just after—contrasts the innocence of His sleep with the growing panic of the disciples. The Greek verb used here is also employed in the Greek translation of the Old Testament (Septuagint) to describe natural sleep.
G0879.portee: This passage shows Jesus in His human reality: He needs rest like any man. His deep sleep also reveals His trust in God the Father—He sleeps without fear, knowing that God is keeping Him. For the reader, it is an invitation to cast their anxieties on the Lord and to find rest in Him, even in the midst of the storm.

sens: Unable to speak or does not speak
Not producing any intelligible or meaningful sound
Devoid of reason or consciousness
G0880.detail:
1. The primary sense is literal: one who does not speak, who is voiceless. The lamb led to slaughter in Acts 8:32 is described as mute before the one who shears it — it does not cry out, it does not defend itself with words. It is the image of silent submission.
2. The word also applies to that which has no meaning or sense: a "tongue that is intelligible" in 1 Corinthians 14:10 refers to a language that makes sense, as opposed to sounds without content. Idols are "mute" in 1 Corinthians 12:2: they do not speak, they communicate nothing, they are inert and devoid of power.
3. Among animals, mute emphasizes the absence of reason: the donkey in 2 Peter 2:16 is mute, it has no voice — and it is precisely the miracle that it speaks to stop the folly of the prophet Balaam.
G0880.origine: The word comes from the root "phōnē" (voice, sound). The prefix "a-" means "without." Mute literally means "without voice." In Hebrew, this word often translates terms related to silence or the absence of speech, as in the passage about the Servant in Isaiah who does not cry out.
G0880.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Greek New Testament. It describes very diverse realities: speechless creatures (the lamb, the donkey), powerless objects (the idols), and even sounds without meaning (the intelligible tongues). In each case, it is the absence of the ability to communicate, to signify, or to act that is emphasized. The context of Acts 8:32 cites Isaiah and highlights the humility of the Servant who does not defend Himself. In 1 Corinthians 12 and 14, Paul uses this word to show the spiritual uselessness of certain practices.
G0880.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that certain things — like idols — cannot speak, cannot save, cannot guide. It invites us to recognize that only the living Word of God has meaning and power. The image of the mute lamb also refers to the humility of Christ who, without defending Himself, offered Himself for us.

sens: King of Judah in the 8th century B.C.
G0881.detail: Ahaz is a king of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus according to the Gospel of Matthew. He is the son of Jotham and the father of Hezekiah, placing him in the royal lineage leading to Christ.
G0881.origine: The Hebrew name אָחָז (Ahaz) literally means "he has seized" or "he has taken hold." It is a theophoric name that expresses a divine action. In Hebrew, it is the same name found in the Old Testament, particularly in the books of Kings and Chronicles where his actions as king are reported.
G0881.emploi: Ahaz appears once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:9, in the genealogy of Jesus. Matthew mentions him to establish the continuity of the royal lineage of Judah that leads to Jesus Christ. In the Old Testament, Ahaz is an important figure: he was a king of Judah (circa 735-715 B.C.) whose story is recounted in 2 Kings 16 and 2 Chronicles 28. These texts present him as a king who often misgoverned and turned away from the path of God.
G0881.portee: The presence of Ahaz in the genealogy of Jesus reminds us of a central truth of the Gospel: God has not rejected His promise to the house of David, even when the kings made serious mistakes. This shows that God's grace extends to all the links in the chain leading to the Savior, regardless of their flaws.

sens: Roman province in southern Greece
Region including Corinth and its surroundings
Territory evangelized by Paul and his companions
G0882.detail:
1. Achaia is a Roman province created in 146 BC after the conquest of Greece. It covers the southern part of the Greek peninsula and includes the major city of Corinth, where Paul established a thriving church. Gallio, a Roman proconsul, administers justice there (Acts 18:12).
2. The region hosts the first converts from the Greek world and becomes an important center of the emerging Christian faith. The household of Stephanas is described as "the firstfruits of Achaia," meaning the first fruits of evangelization in this area (1 Corinthians 16:15).
3. The churches of Achaia demonstrate remarkable generosity: they contribute to the poor in Jerusalem with an eagerness that inspires other churches (Romans 15:26, 2 Corinthians 9:2).
G0882.origine: The Greek name "Achaia" comes from the ancient historical region of the Peloponnese populated by the Achaeans. By the time of the New Testament, the term applies to the Roman province officially established after the destruction of Corinth in 146 BC and its reconstruction a century later.
G0882.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's letters and in Acts. Paul travels through Achaia during his second missionary journey (Acts 18-19), establishes the church in Corinth, and stays there. The letters to the Corinthians and Thessalonians are addressed to the churches in this province. Achaia represents a vital center of Paul's mission in Greece, where the Gospel takes root quickly and where believers are noted for their enthusiasm and generosity.
G0882.portee: Achaia illustrates the rapidity with which the Gospel spread in pagan territory and how young churches can become models of faith and sharing. For the reader, it serves as a reminder that the heart of God's action in the first century was shifting from the Jewish world to the Greek and Roman world, and that Christian generosity transcends geographical boundaries.

sens: man from Corinth, companion of Paul
G0883.detail: Achaicus is a Christian from Corinth, mentioned alongside Stephanas and Fortunatus as someone who visited Paul and comforted him (1 Corinthians 16:17). His Greek name suggests that he comes from Achaia, the region in southern Greece where Corinth was located. Along with his two companions, he "supplied for the absence" of the Church of Corinth to the apostle: their presence compensated, in a way, for the fact that the entire Church could not be there.
G0883.origine: Achaicus is a Greek name derived from Achaia (Ἀχαΐα), the name of the Roman province in southern Greece. The suffix -ικός (as in "French" coming from "France") indicates origin or belonging: Achaicus literally means "one who is from Achaia." It is a patronymic or ethnic name, very common in the Greco-Roman world to designate a person by their region of origin.
G0883.emploi: Achaicus appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul's first letter to the Corinthians. In 1 Corinthians 16:17, Paul welcomes him along with Stephanas and Fortunatus, who have come to join him and bring him joy. In 1 Corinthians 16:24, Paul greets them again at the end of his letter. These brief mentions show that Achaicus was a respected and active member of the Church of Corinth, devoted to Paul and engaged in apostolic service.
G0883.portee: Achaicus embodies the mutual love and practical support that characterize the early Christian community. His simple act — traveling to visit Paul and encourage him — shows how each member of the Church, even unknown, can fill a gap and bring comfort to an apostle. It is a reminder that faith is never solitary: it is lived in community, through small acts of concrete devotion.

sens: One who does not recognize a received benefit
Who lacks gratitude toward God
Who has no appreciation or kindness
G0884.detail:
1. An ingrate is one who receives a good, a favor, or help, but does not recognize it and does not give thanks to the one who gave it. In Luke 6:35, Jesus speaks of God who is "good to the ungrateful," meaning who gives His blessings (rain, sunshine) even to those who are not thankful to Him.
2. The word also describes the attitude of one who does not give thanks to God for His gifts. In 2 Timothy 3:2, the ingrate appears among the characteristics of sinful men in the last days, alongside selfishness and ungodliness: it is the refusal to recognize that everything comes from God.
3. More broadly, ingratitude is a form of insensitivity to goodness: it closes the heart to appreciation and kindness toward the one who has given.
G0884.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "grace" or "favor" (χάρις). The negative prefix "a-" (without) creates the opposite: literally "without grace." An ingrate is therefore one who ignores, rejects, or misuses the grace received. This word expresses the voluntary or involuntary forgetfulness of a benefit.
G0884.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 6:35, Jesus uses it to describe those who receive God's goodness without recognizing it: God loves and blesses even the ungrateful, out of pure mercy. In 2 Timothy 3:2, Paul places it in a list of moral faults of the last days, as an expression of sin that turns man away from gratitude toward God and pushes him toward selfishness. Ingratitude is thus a sin that isolates from the true heart of God.
G0884.portee: Recognizing that we are all potential ingrates: we receive God's blessings every day without always thanking Him. The word encourages us to cultivate gratitude toward God and toward those who do good to us. It is also a call to imitate God's mercy, who continues to love even those who do not recognize Him.

sens: Character in the genealogy of Jesus according to Matthew
G0885.detail: Achim is an ancestor of Jesus in the Davidic lineage. He appears only once in the New Testament, in the genealogy that Matthew presents at the beginning of his Gospel, where he is listed as the son of Sadok and the father of Elihud.
G0885.origine: The name Achim is the Greek form of a Hebrew name (probably related to "Jehoiakim" or an abbreviated form). It fits within the Hebrew tradition of theophoric names (containing a reference to God), although its exact meaning is uncertain in our sources.
G0885.emploi: Achim is mentioned only once in the New Testament: in Matthew 1:14, in the genealogy of Jesus. This genealogical list traces back from Jesus to Abraham and establishes His legitimacy as heir to the throne of David. Achim represents one of the links in this genealogical chain, although we know nothing else about his life or deeds.

sens: That which has not been built, shaped, or created by human hands
That which surpasses human craftsmanship or work
Figuratively: that which is spiritual, divine, operated by God alone
G0886.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to that which has not been constructed or shaped by human hands. Jesus speaks of a temple "not made by human hands" that He will build in three days (Mark 14:58): it is not a stone building erected by workers, but something of an entirely different order, a spiritual reality.
2. Paul uses the image to describe our heavenly dwelling: "an eternal dwelling not made by human hands" (2 Corinthians 5:1). He contrasts the earthly, perishable body with an eternal habitation of divine origin that only God can provide.
3. Figuratively and spiritually, Paul speaks of the "circumcision made without hands" (Colossians 2:11): it is not the physical act of a knife, but the invisible work of the Spirit that strips the heart of sin. The word emphasizes that true transformation comes from God, not from human effort.
G0886.origine: The Greek word is formed from three elements: the negation α- ("not"), χείρ ("hand"), and ποιητός ("made, manufactured"). It literally means "not-made-by-hand." This compound construction sharply contrasts divine work with human fabrication: what comes from God does not bear the mark of human hands.
G0886.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always to express a spiritual reality that escapes human capability. Mark reports Jesus' words about a temple not made by human hands (Mark 14:58), announcing His resurrection as a living edifice. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 5:1 to encourage believers by showing that God prepares a very real, though invisible, eternal dwelling. In Colossians 2:11, the word qualifies the spiritual circumcision of the heart, the transformative work of Christ that no physical or human effort can accomplish. In each use, the word marks the difference between what man can do and what only God can do.
G0886.portee: This word reminds believers that true spiritual transformation does not come from our efforts or external rituals, but from the action of God alone. It invites trust: our salvation, our circumcision of the heart, our eternal dwelling do not depend on human hands, but on the mighty hand of God. It is a comfort and a call to seek the essential in the spiritual realm, not in appearance or carnal work.

sens: A kind of fog or veil that obscures vision
A temporary or permanent loss of sight
Figuratively, ignorance or mental confusion
G0887.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a fog or mist that envelops the eyes and prevents clear sight. It is a darkness that floats before the gaze, like an opaque veil. In Acts 13:11, the magician Ananias is struck by this darkness, rendering him blind: "immediately darkness and gloom fell upon him."
2. By extension, the word describes blindness or an inability to see, whether temporary or permanent. It is not merely a physical loss of light, but a deprivation of sight itself, so that the affected person must be guided, "groping."
3. In a broader sense, it can evoke moral or spiritual darkness—ignorance and confusion that blind the mind. Although the term is rarely used in this sense in the New Testament, the poetic image of the veil and fog suits this kind of invisible blindness.
G0887.origine: The Greek word ἀχλύς comes from an Indo-European root that evokes darkness and disturbance. The term is rare in Greek scripture and in secular literature; it belongs to a poetic and imagery vocabulary. The feminine noun suggests a concrete reality that "falls" upon the eyes like a palpable presence.
G0887.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 13:11, during the miracle where Paul strikes the magician Ananias with blindness, who opposes the Gospel. The context is that of divine judgment: sight is taken away as punishment and warning. The term "darkness" (ἀχλύς) is associated with "gloom" to emphasize the totality of the punishment. This unique occurrence shows the use of the word in a decisive moment of apostolic history, where the power of the name of Jesus overcomes magic and opposition.
G0887.portee: This account teaches the reality of God's judgment on those who resist His Gospel. The image of darkness suddenly falling upon the magician's eyes also symbolizes how sin and opposition to Christ trap a person in darkness, depriving them of the light of the Word. For the reader, this serves as a reminder of the urgency to turn toward the truth rather than persist in unbelief.

sens: That which serves no purpose, has no utility or productive value
That which has not fulfilled its expected duty or function
That which, in a moral sense, deserves no reward for its work
G0888.detail:
1. Literally, this word refers to that which cannot render any service, that which has no utility. It is a servant who is worthless in his function (Matthew 25:30).
2. More specifically, it is one who had a task to accomplish but did not fulfill it as he should have. The servant did not become useless through absolute laziness, but because he did not take advantage of what was given to him.
3. In a moral and spiritual sense, it is the absence of benefit or profit: the disciple who has obeyed the commandments cannot boast of having earned a reward, for he has only done his duty—this work itself adds nothing to his value; he remains a servant with no claim to glory (Luke 17:10).
G0888.origine: The word comes from the Greek root that means "useful" or "that which brings profit" (χρεῖος). The prefix ἀ- (negation) denies it: hence "without utility." This word translates into Greek the Hebrew ideas of what is despicable or worthless, particularly in passages where the Old Testament speaks of what is rejected or ineffective.
G0888.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew and Luke, in parables or teachings of Christ about the Kingdom. In Matthew 25:30, it is the unfaithful servant of the parable of the talents who is called "useless servant": the one who buried his talent instead of making it fruitful, and who ends up cast out. In Luke 17:10, Jesus teaches His disciples that even after having fulfilled all the commandments, they should not be proud: they remain useless servants, for doing their duty is never enough to earn grace. Both contexts revolve around responsibility, faithfulness, and judgment.
G0888.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on their responsibility before God. Not being useless means making use of the gifts received and obeying the commandments—not to earn salvation, but out of gratitude for grace. It also reminds us of humility: even our best works are merely our duty to an infinite Master. This word preserves the biblical doctrine: we are never beyond grace, and true value does not come from our merits.

sens: Deprive of value, utility, profit
In a moral sense: corrupt, degrade, cause to lose righteousness
G0889.detail:
1. The verb means to cause something to lose all usefulness or value: to render useless, without profit. The image evokes something that becomes worthless, that no longer serves a purpose.
2. In its moral usage in Romans 3:12, it describes human beings as they turn away from God: they "have turned aside" and become useless, corrupted, incapable of doing good. It is a moral corruption that annihilates the spiritual value of the person.
G0889.origine: The word comes from the root ἄχρεος (achreios), "useless" or "without value." This root itself derives from α- (a-, negation) and χρή (khré), which means "to be useful, to have need." In Hebrew, the New Testament (in its ancient Greek translation) uses this verb to render words like אָלַח (alakh), "to pervert" or "to corrupt." It is a compound word that expresses the idea of losing its original usefulness or value.
G0889.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 3:12. Paul uses it to describe the spiritual state of humanity: all humans, without exception, have "turned aside" from God and "have become corrupted." The context is that of Paul's demonstration that no one possesses their own righteousness. The verb expresses not only the turning away from God but the complete loss of moral value that results from it.
G0889.portee: This word reminds the believer of a humbling truth: without God, we are spiritually useless and corrupted. It highlights the urgency of divine grace in Jesus Christ, who alone can restore us. Understanding this radical corruption drives the Christian to appreciate even more their free salvation in Christ and to recognize that there is no merit in themselves.

sens: Having no utility, serving no purpose
Not fulfilling the role expected of it
Being unproductive or without practical value
G0890.detail:
1. The word describes at first degree something that has no use, that renders no service: it is the opposite of a useful object or person. In Philemon 11, Onesimus was "useless" — probably a runaway slave who was not working for his master.
2. In a broader sense, it is what does not fulfill its expected function, what disappoints the expectation of utility. An useless servant is one who does not accomplish their task.
3. Figuratively, the word can qualify a life, a work, or an act that produces no lasting or beneficial fruit — it is the absence of value in the moral or spiritual realm.
G0890.origine: The Greek word ἄχρηστος is formed from the privative prefix "a-" ("without") and χρῆσις ("use, utility"). The word literally describes what is "without use." It directly opposes εὔχρηστος ("useful, practical"). In Hebrew, the Old Testament speaks of what has no "desire" or "pleasure," that is, what has no value or profit.
G0890.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in the letter to Philemon. Paul uses it in verse 11 to describe Onesimus's former condition — literally, his name means "useful" in Greek, but he was not truly so until his conversion. Paul plays on this contrast: Onesimus, formerly useless, now becomes truly useful. This vocabulary of utility and service runs throughout the epistle and emphasizes the transformation that faith brings to a person.
G0890.portee: This word reminds us that our value before God does not depend on our productivity or human effectiveness. Like Onesimus, we may be "useless" in our own eyes or in the eyes of others, but grace makes us useful — that is, capable of serving and contributing to the Kingdom of God. It is a call to see in everyone a potential transformed by faith.

sens: up to a point, a limit in time
up to a point, a limit in space
up to a degree, a measure or intensity
until the moment when (temporal conjunction)
G0891.detail:
1. Marks the temporal limit: the action or state lasts and stops at a specific moment. Example: "they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark" (Matthew 24:38) — people live normally until the moment the flood comes.

2. Marks the spatial limit: up to a place, to a geographical point. The word of God "is living, powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword; it pierces even to the division of soul and spirit" (Hebrews 4:12) — it reaches the most intimate depths.

3. Marks intensity or measure: "until death" (Revelation 2:10) means to the extreme point, to the highest degree.

4. Introduces a temporal conjunction: "until" indicates the moment when something will cease or change. "A part of Israel has hardened, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in" (Romans 11:25) — this state lasts until that event occurs.
G0891.origine: The word comes from an archaic Greek root. In classical times, the form ἄχρις is also found. It is a very ancient preposition that fundamentally expresses the idea of reaching a limit or boundary. It governs the genitive (the case of the complement). It is close to the word μέχρι, which has the same meaning and is used interchangeably.
G0891.emploi: Ἄχρι appears 49 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts, Paul's epistles, and Revelation. As a preposition (senses 1 to 3), it is used with a genitive complement: "until the appointed time" (Galatians 4:2), "until the end" (Revelation 2:26), "until this word" (Acts 22:22). As a conjunction (sense 4), it introduces a temporal clause with a verb in the aorist subjunctive or indicative: "until another king arose" (Acts 7:18), "until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in" (Romans 11:25). In Hebrews 3:13, it can also mean "while": "as long as it is said: Today."
G0891.portee: This word roots the Christian faith in the concrete of time and space. It reminds us that God acts in history: His promises are not vague; they have limits and moments. For the believer, "until the end" (Revelation 2:26) or "until death" (Revelation 2:10) calls for faithfulness and perseverance. It helps us see that our life is not infinite, that it has boundaries, and that our commitment to God must last until that defined term.

sens: The light husks and debris that remain after separating the grains of wheat or barley
Figuratively, that which is worthless, that which must be rejected or destroyed
G0892.detail:
1. Straw is the light residue of grain after threshing and winnowing — the broken stalks and husks that cannot be eaten. In the imagery that John the Baptist uses in Matthew 3:12, he describes the Lord who "will clear his threshing floor," meaning He will separate the good grain from the rest, just as a farmer uses a winnowing fork to let the straw fall while the heavier grain remains.
2. Figuratively, straw represents what is useless, worthless, and destined for destruction. John the Baptist uses it to speak of the fate of the reprobate: while the wheat (the elect, those who believe) will be gathered into the barn (heaven), the straw will be "burned with unquenchable fire" (Luke 3:17), meaning delivered to eternal judgment.
G0892.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes what is light and volatile — straw blows away in the wind, unlike grain which falls. In Hebrew, תֶּבֶן (teben) refers to both straw and chaff. The image is very ancient: it speaks of the separation of the precious from the worthless, the durable from the perishable.
G0892.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two parallel accounts of John the Baptist's preaching. It appears in the same baptismal context, where John announces the coming of the Messiah who will judge: He will take a winnowing fork to separate the elect from the rest. It is a very vivid agricultural image for a Palestinian audience familiar with grain threshing. The meaning remains the same: the material straw is used for a spiritual comparison regarding final judgment.
G0892.portee: This image of straw and wheat speaks to the heart of the believer: it reminds us that our lives will be judged according to their spiritual value. It invites us to examine whether we are wheat — whether our faith and works are genuine and enduring — or merely straw, light and perishable. It is a call to seriousness in the face of God's judgment.

sens: God in His nature: incapable of lying, deceiving, faithful to His word
That which is true, authentic, without deception
G0893.detail:
1. The word describes God Himself as fundamentally incapable of lying or deception. It is an affirmation of His deep nature: God cannot deviate from the truth, He cannot go back on His promises (Titus 1:2). This impossibility is not a limitation but the perfection of His character.
2. By extension, it also qualifies that which is true and trustworthy, without hidden lies: a word, a promise that deceives no one.
G0893.origine: The word comes from the prefix "a-" (privative) and "pseudês" which means lie or falsehood. Literally, it means "without lie." In Hebrew, a similar image is found with the word "emet" (truth), which evokes what is stable, enduring, firm — what can be reached and relied upon.
G0893.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:2, where Paul affirms that God promised eternal life before the ages began. This is a crucial affirmation: it means that God's promises are not capricious or changeable, but anchored in His very essence. This assurance is directed to Christians who base their faith on biblical promises and must know that they rest on God's immutable nature.
G0893.portee: For the believer, this word is a source of deep trust. It reminds us that we do not serve a capricious or deceptive God, but one who cannot lie. This gives absolute solidity to every promise of the Gospel and every call to faith: our hopes rest on someone completely trustworthy.

sens: a bitter plant from which a liquor is made
the bitter and unpleasant taste of this plant
a moral or spiritual bitterness
G0894.detail:
1. Wormwood is a real plant, well-known in the East, that produces an extremely bitter substance. A drink (wormwood liquor) is made from it that has the same characteristic bitter taste.

2. The word also designates the bitter taste itself, this unpleasant sensation: something that is repugnant to the palate and cannot be swallowed without disgust.

3. The Bible uses wormwood figuratively to evoke moral or spiritual bitterness: sin, misfortune, or the bitter consequences of unfaithfulness. In Revelation 8:11, the water turning into wormwood symbolizes the misfortune and death that strike men through divine judgment.
G0894.origine: The Greek word ἄψινθος (apsinthos) comes from a root that evokes the idea of burning or drying up, related to the sharp flavor of the plant. It is an ancient word, borrowed from Semitic languages (the Hebrew lafga). The French word "absinthe" directly derives from the Greek. The plant itself was used in medicine and cooking in the Mediterranean antiquity.
G0894.emploi: The word ἄψινθος (wormwood) appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 8:11. It is the only use of the word in the complete Bible provided. In this passage, wormwood is not mentioned as a mere plant, but as the symbolic name of a star that falls from heaven during divine judgment. The waters of rivers and springs turn into wormwood, making the water bitter and poisonous: this causes the death of many men. The word functions here as an image of divine judgment and its disastrous consequences.
G0894.portee: For the Christian reading Revelation, wormwood reminds us that God's judgment is not a distant or abstract act, but a reality that makes bitter and brings death. It also evokes the classic biblical idea that bitterness is the mark of sin and distance from God: those who stray from Him taste not sweetness, but bitterness. It is a call to vigilance and faithfulness in the face of the judgments that God reserves.

sens: That which has no life, that is not living
That which lacks soul or vital spirit
That which cannot feel, act, or move by itself
G0895.detail:
1. An inanimate object is simply devoid of life in the biological sense: it does not exist, it does not breathe, it does not move by itself. This is the case with a flute or a harp (1 Corinthians 14:7), which are manufactured musical instruments.
2. In Greek thought, the soul (ψυχή, "psychē") is what animates a living being and allows it to feel and act. An inanimate object lacks this: it cannot will or feel.
3. By extension, inanimate characterizes that which has no capacity for autonomous expression or intelligent communication — unlike a living being that can spontaneously make itself understood.
G0895.origine: The Greek word ἄψυχος is composed of the negative prefix ἀ- ("not, without") and the noun ψυχή ("soul, life"). It literally means "without soul." In classical and biblical Greek, the soul denotes the vital principle that distinguishes the living from dead objects or mere material things. This word expresses the fundamental contrast between the living and the inert.
G0895.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 14:7, where Paul uses it to refer to musical instruments — the flute and the harp. His argument is that even these inanimate objects produce distinct sounds, and without this distinction, no one would understand what is played. Paul uses this term to emphasize that all communication, even that of lifeless objects, must have clarity to be useful: all the more so, the word and spiritual gifts among Christians must be intelligible to edify the assembly.
G0895.portee: This word reminds us that true life, in the biblical sense, is the privilege of living beings and the soul. It also helps us reflect on the quality of our words and our testimony: as Paul suggests, even a simple flute must speak clearly to be of any use. The gifts of the Spirit in the Church must also be exercised with intelligence and clarity to truly edify the brothers and sisters.

sens: pagan deity worshiped by the ancient peoples of the Near East
idol or false god to whom the Israelites sometimes offered worship in rebellion against the true God
G0896.detail:
1. Baal is the name of a deity worshiped in the religions of the neighboring peoples of Israel, particularly among the Phoenicians and Canaanites. It is a central figure in their pantheon, associated with fertility and rain. The word literally means "lord" in Hebrew.
2. In the history of Israel, some kings and the people turned away from the God of Abraham to worship Baal and his counterparts, provoking God's anger. The Apostle Paul cites this fact in Romans 11:4 to remind that even in the time of the prophet Elijah, when almost all of Israel seemed to have bowed the knee to Baal, God had reserved a faithful remnant: "seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to Baal." This is a sign of God's grace toward those who persevere in true faith.
G0896.origine: Baal comes from the Hebrew בַּעַל (ba'al), which literally means "lord" or "master." It was the name of one or more deities of the Canaanite world, worshiped by the surrounding peoples. The Hebrew word also designated a owner or master of a house in a secular sense, but in a religious context, it became the proper name of an opposing spiritual power. The prophets of Israel, like Elijah, vigorously opposed the worship of Baal.
G0896.emploi: Baal appears only once in the Greek New Testament: Romans 11:4, where Paul cites the passage from 1 Kings 19:18 describing the crisis of the prophet Elijah. At that time, King Ahab and Queen Jezebel had imposed the worship of Baal in Israel, and the people had largely adopted it. Paul uses this historical reference to show that God never completely abandons His people: even in widespread apostasy, He preserves a remnant of faithful ones who refuse to bow the knee to false gods. The mention of Baal in Romans 11 reminds Christians of the spiritual reality of idolatrous temptation and divine faithfulness.
G0896.portee: The example of Baal invites Christians to reflect on the temptation of spiritual idolatry: substituting false gods for God — wealth, success, reputation, passions. Paul teaches us that even when the majority seems to stray from the truth, God remains faithful to those who cling to Him. This is a source of encouragement and humility: not to follow the crowd, but to persevere in true faith.

sens: Capital of the Babylonian empire in ancient Mesopotamia
Place of deportation for the people of Judah in the 6th century B.C.
Symbol of the political-religious power hostile to God
Prophetic designation of Rome in Revelation
G0897.detail:
1. Babylon is primarily the great capital of the Babylonian empire, located in present-day Iraq, on the Euphrates River. It is a real city, one of the most powerful in the ancient world, known for its architectural wonders and grandeur.

2. In the 6th century B.C., King Nebuchadnezzar II deported the people of Judah there after the destruction of Jerusalem. It is this dramatic event that Matthew recalls by structuring his genealogy of Christ into three periods of fourteen generations, one of which is "from the deportation to Babylon" (Matthew 1:17).

3. In the prophecies of Revelation, Babylon becomes a symbol of any empire that opposes God, blending political power and false religious cults. It represents the seduction of the world and its idolatry: "Babylon the great, who has made all nations drink the wine of the wrath of her fornication" (Revelation 14:8).

4. Many interpreters see in Babylon, in Revelation, a prophetic designation of Rome, which oppressed the early Church. Some also believe that 1 Peter 5:13 uses this name symbolically to refer to Rome, from where Peter was writing to the persecuted Church.
G0897.origine: The name Babylon comes from the Babylonian "Bab-ili," which means "Gate of God." This name evokes the pride of a city that claims to be the gate leading to the divine, but which strays from the true God. In the Greek Scriptures, Babylon appears as the counterpart of corrupt Jerusalem: while Jerusalem was to be the holy city of the true God, Babylon embodies political and religious idolatry. Revelation takes up this contrast by opposing heavenly Jerusalem to Babylon the great.
G0897.emploi: Babylon first appears in the Gospel of Matthew (1:11, 12, 17) as a major historical landmark: it marks the turning point of the exile, divided by Matthew into three equal generations. Acts 7:43 alludes to it as a place of future deportation, applying an ancient word to the fate of the unfaithful people. In Revelation (14:8; 16:19; 17:5; 18:2, 10, 21), Babylon becomes a central prophetic figure: it symbolizes the false religious and political power that opposes the kingdom of God and will ultimately fall. Finally, 1 Peter 5:13 uses this name, either literally for Rome or symbolically to refer to the Church in exile in a hostile land.
G0897.portee: Babylon reminds believers that even exile, even the deportation of God's children, is not outside the control of the sovereign God: Matthew makes it a natural step toward Christ. It also teaches that human empires, no matter how powerful, last only for a time and fall before God. For the persecuted Church, seeing Rome under the name Babylon is a consolation: the present power that oppresses is but a beast that will be defeated, while the kingdom of God alone endures forever.

sens: A step, a physical degree
A position, a level in a hierarchy
A social or ecclesiastical status
G0898.detail:
1. The word βαθμός primarily denotes a step or degree — that is, a stage that one ascends or descends, like the steps of a staircase or a sundial. The image is of the foot resting on each level to progress.

2. In a figurative sense, it refers to a position, a degree in a progression: what places someone at a certain level in relation to others. In 1 Timothy 3:13, deacons who serve well "gain an honorable rank" — the word denotes the status they earn, the esteem they receive in the Church, like an elevation in the order of the community.

3. This rank is particularly a status in ecclesiastical life: it is the recognized place, the spiritual and social credit that a servant of Christ obtains through faithfulness and integrity.
G0898.origine: The word comes from the root βαίνω (baïnô), which means "to walk" or "to go." Βαθμός is formed on this image of the step, the degree one crosses while walking. It is an Ionic word (an ancient Greek dialect); the more common form is βασμός. The term expresses the idea of progression, of gradual ascent — each step elevates us by one degree.
G0898.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Timothy 3:13. Paul uses it to speak of the "honorable rank" that deacons acquire when they serve well in their office. It is not a human promotion, but a spiritual recognition and assurance (confidence) that comes from a life of faithful service. The word values the position of the deacon not as a power, but as an honor earned through integrity — a status of respect and trust accumulated through good work.
G0898.portee: This passage shows that faithful service rendered in the Church bears fruit: not only in terms of heavenly reward but also here and now, in spiritual credit and assurance in faith. The Christian who gives everything for his ministry does not only become better; he also gains a stable and honored place within the community, and a trust rooted in life with Christ.

sens: vertical thickness of a layer of earth or water
the abyss, the immensity of the ocean
that which is mysterious, unfathomable, hidden from sight
the intensity or extremity of a state
G0899.detail:
1. Depth primarily refers to the vertical extent of a solid or liquid substance: it is the distance between the surface and the bottom. In Matthew 13:5 and Mark 4:5, the seed that fell on rocky ground cannot sprout due to insufficient depth of soil — the image is that of a thin and unwelcoming layer.
2. In Luke 5:4, "water" literally translates as "depth" — the word refers to the deep water of the lake, where the net can catch fish. It is the liquid element itself, especially when it concerns the open sea.
3. Metaphorically, the word expresses what escapes human understanding. In Romans 11:33, the "depth" of the riches of God evokes inexhaustible and mysterious treasures, and in 1 Corinthians 2:10, the "depths of God" are the secret divine plans that only the Spirit can explore.
4. The word can finally qualify the extreme intensity of a situation: in 2 Corinthians 8:2, the "deep poverty" of certain Christians expresses a radical and heartbreaking misery.
G0899.origine: The Greek word βάθος comes from a root expressing the idea of descending, going down — hence its primary and concrete meaning of depth or thickness. It is the opposite of "height." In Hebrew, it corresponds to words like מְצוּלָה (abyss) or תַּחְתִּי (lower, deep), both of which evoke the extent or obscurity of hidden and distant things.
G0899.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament. It is first used in a concrete and agricultural sense (Matthew 13:5; Mark 4:5), then to designate the extent of water or the sea (Luke 5:4). However, the Bible primarily uses it figuratively: to speak of the infinite dimensions of God or His love (Romans 8:39; Ephesians 3:18), the divine secrets revealed by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:10), or the extreme intensity of a human experience such as poverty (2 Corinthians 8:2) or wisdom (Romans 11:33). This progression from the concrete to the spiritual is characteristic of biblical language.
G0899.portee: This word invites the Christian to contemplate the infinite dimension of God — His riches, wisdom, and love know no bounds. But it also confronts him with his natural inability to fathom these depths: only the Spirit of God can reveal them to us. For the life of faith, this means that we are called to surrender to a God whose thoughts and ways infinitely surpass us, as Romans 11:33 expresses with wonder.
